extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/history; journalists interested in 19th-century newspaper practice
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what made newspapers successful or influential in the U.S. during the Civil War and Reconstruction era (c.1860–1872), covering news-gathering, editorial practice, features, business models, and ethics. Useful for assessing historical newspapers or extracting historic journalistic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness and popular appeal of news
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's news must be 'the freshest, most interesting and sprightliest current,' produced with resources spared to make it what the great mass of the people want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in rapid, wide-ranging newsgathering; prioritize stories that feel immediate and engaging to broad audiences. Example: the Sun's advertisement (1870) claiming freshness as key to popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price and circulation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success could depend on pricing (e.g., the Sun's two-cent price vs. four-cent rivals) combined with content strategy to grow circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower cover price can attract mass readership but may require adjustments in pages, advertising, or production costs. Price alone is not sufficient; content must back up the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and sensationalism as newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News that is 'pert, novel, and sometimes sensational' sells; stories emphasizing the unexpected or unusual are more likely to attract readers ('dog bites man' vs. 'man bites dog' adage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek novelty and surprising angles; avoid reporting only commonplace occurrences. Anti-pattern: dull repetition of routine items without an angle of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Short articles interesting for human texture rather than the public importance of the subject — e.g., portraits of a Chinese laundryman, witty policeman, lost child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest pieces must be well written to avoid banality; rely on vivid, empathetic, or amusing detail. Without good writing, such features become trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of writing (style and voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing — colorful, witty, zestful prose — is a principal contribution to newspaper success (the Sun's chief contribution was good writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a distinct, readable voice across reporting and editorials; train staff in lively prose. Example: Dana's emphasis on writing and his editorial team's short, incisive essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment in staff, training, and employment conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage bright young reporters (often college graduates) with good salaries, fairly assured tenure, and systematic training to produce superior journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize hiring and retention, mentorship from experienced editors, and formalized training systems to raise reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial-page incisiveness and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials that are short, amusing essays with incisiveness and wit (on fads, language, social questions) can distinguish a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise, sharp editorials to engage readers; balance wit with responsibility. Anti-pattern: excessive frivolity that undermines influence on serious issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of slashing attacks and personal cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: While slashing, whimsical attacks can entertain, they 'were sometimes cruel and malicious' and could be called blackguardism; frivolous positions on important questions reduced actual influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous personal attacks and irrelevant frivolity; weigh long-term credibility against short-term sensational effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and political stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers evolved from party organs toward greater independence; independence from party bonds and willingness to criticize nominal allies increased credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for factual reporting and the ability to criticize parties when warranted. Financial or partisan ties that compromise coverage are damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triumph of the news principle (news over editorials)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the penny papers onward, news became the leading function of the newspaper; the success and rank of a paper depend chiefly on its ability to get and exhibit the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize newsroom resources on newsgathering, verification, and presentation. Editorials matter less for circulation than timely, full reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting as a skilled craft ('reporting is a high art')
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter — not the editor — often becomes the 'ruling genius' for readers; skilled, faithful reporting and thorough coverage (e.g., Tribune's Franco-Prussian War work) are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value experienced correspondents, thoroughness, and methodological rigor in reporting; invest resources (including money) for comprehensive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of new technologies for timeliness (telegraph and cable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of telegraph and submarine cable fastered international and domestic news flow; timely transmission became a competitive edge despite high costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit fast transmission means to break and update stories; be mindful of cable/dispatch costs and contractual arrangements (e.g., first extensive cable dispatch costing $6,500 in gold).

rubrics_metrics.name: News-sharing organizations and syndication agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements (e.g., Associated Press) concentrated wire news; regional associations and negotiated concessions distributed costs and reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperate regionally to obtain equitable access to wire news; resist monopolistic practices that disadvantage sections. Reforms and regional groups can rebalance access and charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview technique and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: The interview became a technique to elicit intimate details of public figures but was criticized as invasion of privacy and sometimes as staged or 'joint product' of hacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to add color and first-person detail, but verify authenticity and respect privacy. Beware of manufactured interviews or reliance on political handlers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms of 'personal journalism' and overwriting ('Jenkins')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'personal journalist' who reported trivial society detail and reporters who overwrote insignificant items were frequently condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overwriting and trivial social puffery; maintain relevance and restraint in features about private lives. Readers prefer substantive items over flowery, insignificant copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative/crusading journalism (use of official records and persistence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crusades against corruption (e.g., Times and Harper's Weekly against the Tweed Ring) relied on acquisition of records, persistent exposure, and coordination (including cartoons) to produce civic consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use documentary evidence, meticulous analysis of public records, and multimedia (e.g., cartoons) to expose corruption; expect pushback, hush-money attempts, and the need for sustained public pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of visual satire (political cartoons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartoons (Thomas Nast) could be decisive in swaying public opinion and materially aid campaigns against corruption, despite threats and intimidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strong, clear visual satire responsibly as a persuasive tool; be prepared for retaliation and protect contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business independence and vulnerability to financial influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers could be compromised by hush-money, advertising contracts, or patronage (e.g., many papers on the Ring's payroll), which weakened crusading potential and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard editorial independence from financial coercion; transparency and refusal to accept corrupt payments underpin public trust. Example: Jones's refusal of $5,000,000 to suppress records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility and editorial manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The public wanted 'temperate, dignified, gentlemanly explanation and criticism' rather than highly personal vituperation among papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professional civility even in adversarial coverage; excessive personal attacks undermine the newspaper's dignity and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of features (poetry, wit, humor) to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekly miscellanies and some dailies published poetry, humorous essays, and miscellany; such material could be a distinguishing feature (e.g., Evening Post's verse, Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper's serial fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance hard news with literary and entertaining features appropriate to the paper's format and audience; weeklies often carry more miscellany, while some dailies emphasize news.
